headline: Expat Salary Floor Doubles to RM20K from 1 June 2026; The Pipeline Question Remains
context: From 1 June 2026, the Employment Pass Category I minimum rose from RM10,000 to RM20,000. Category III is capped at 5 years; the replacement-plan requirement was deferred to 1 January 2027. The policy aims to focus expatriate hiring on high-impact expertise.

changes.summary: Correction: Singapore's Employment Pass minimum corrected from SGD5,000 to SGD5,600 (SGD6,200 in financial services). Replaced the 3,000-graduate figure with about 6,600 E&E graduates a year.

Correction: at BNM's 30 Mar 2026 rate, Singapore's EP floors of SGD5,600 and SGD6,200 come to about RM17,400 and RM19,300, both below RM20,000; earlier editions said about RM18,500 and RM20,500. They apply at age 23 and under. Update: the replacement-plan rule was deferred to 1 Jan 2027.

cards.big: Malaysia doubles the Category I Employment Pass minimum salary to RM20,000 from 1 June 2026.
cards.sub: Official framing: focus expatriate hiring on high-impact expertise. Replacement plans (training, mentoring, documentation) now start 1 January 2027, after a May 2026 deferral.

cards.big: Semiconductor target: 60,000 highly skilled engineers by 2030, under the National Semiconductor Strategy.
cards.sub: World Bank documents Malaysian brain drain, with Singapore as the main destination. The price-of-replacements lever is separate from the pipeline.

cards.big: The new floor scales differently across firm sizes. DOSM: MSMEs are 39.5% of GDP and 48.7% of employment in 2024.
cards.sub: Category I foreign hires now face double the threshold. The official FAQ says monitoring will use documentation and periodic reports.

cards.big: Singapore's EP floor starts at SGD5,600 (about RM17,400) for most sectors and SGD6,200 (about RM19,300) in finance, for applicants aged 23 and under.
cards.sub: Malaysia's RM20K tops both entry floors. Singapore's rise with age, to SGD10,700 (about RM33,000) at 45 and over outside finance.

cards.big: The salary floor adjusts the price of foreign replacement. The pipeline question (graduates, retention, brain-drain destinations) is a separate set of policies.
Protecting Malaysian jobs is a legitimate aim. The risk is that protection without parallel pipeline investment becomes paper compliance rather than specialist development.
